Greg, the forwarder called. The container is on schedule, but the original bill of lading still has not arrived in Santos. Where is it?
It was sent by courier on Monday. It should have been sent on the day the vessel sailed, and that one is on us. The tracking number is in my email from this morning.
Thank you. There is a second problem: the value on the invoice does not match the packing list. It must be corrected before Friday, or the goods cannot be released.
That was our mistake too. A corrected invoice can be issued today, and I will have it signed by our finance director before noon.
Good. Now the June run. The volume is confirmed, all of it, so the other half of the space can be booked today, before the rate goes up on the twentieth.
Then the June consignment will be shipped in two containers. But the lead time is longer now: five weeks, not four, because the carrier changed the route.
Five weeks is too long for the plant. Could the second container be rerouted through Paranagua, or can it be expedited if we pay the difference?
Paranagua is possible. I will ask the freight forwarder to price both options, and you will have the numbers in writing before your family meeting on Friday.

Good morning, Maria Claudia, this is Denise Walker at the freight forwarder, calling about the May container from Pittsburgh. The good news first. The vessel is on schedule, and the container is expected in Santos on the twenty-eighth. Now the part that needs your attention. Before the container can be released, three things must be done. The original bill of lading must be sent to our office in Santos by courier, not by email, because customs will not accept a copy. The commercial invoice has to be corrected, because the value on it does not match the value on the packing list. And the import license should be approved before the vessel arrives, not after. If all three are done by Friday, customs clearance usually takes three to five days. If they are not, the container will be moved to a bonded warehouse, and demurrage will be charged from the sixth day, at one hundred and eighty dollars a day. One more thing. The release can be expedited if you pay the priority fee, but I would only do that if the plant really cannot wait. Call me back today and tell me which way you want to go.

The most expensive mistake I have seen in twenty years of logistics cost us one hundred and forty thousand dollars, and it started with a single pallet. We were shipping machine parts to a customer in Chile. The consignment was loaded on a Friday afternoon, in a hurry, because the carrier had moved the cut-off time forward. One pallet was labeled with the wrong product code. It should have been checked against the packing list before the container was sealed, and it was not. Nobody noticed until customs in Chile opened the container, found goods that did not match the documents, and held the entire consignment for three weeks. The customer's line stopped. We paid the demurrage, we paid to expedite a replacement by air, and we paid a penalty on the contract. Here is what I learned. Almost everything in logistics can be fixed, but only before the container is sealed. After that, every mistake must be solved by someone else, in another country, on their schedule. So now one rule is never broken in my warehouse: no container is sealed until the last pallet has been checked by a second person. It costs us twenty minutes. It could have saved us one hundred and forty thousand dollars.

First, before the vessel arrives, you ask the freight forwarder for the full list of what must be done for customs clearance, so that nothing is discovered on the day the container lands. Then, you check that the commercial invoice and the packing list show exactly the same values, because a single mismatch is enough to stop the release. After that, you send the original bill of lading by courier, with a tracking number, since customs will not accept a copy. Next, you confirm how many days of free time you have at the terminal, and from which day demurrage will be charged. Finally, you decide whether the release should be expedited, and you only pay for it when the plant really cannot wait.
